title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
content:
Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.
One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.
In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.
Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race that Axios reported would fundamentally scramble the math on Trump’s AI buildout. According to Bloomberg, Hinojosa’s election has developers facing down the “worst-case scenario.” Texas is the epicenter of the AI boom, Axios noted, and was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028.
Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects as long as it takes to pass laws “tackling impacts on water, electricity, air, and property rights.” Approximately “13 gigawatts of data center capacity” is now exposed, Bloomberg reported. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research warned in a note that Texas projects with “power, permits and steel keep going,” but “those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months,” Bloomberg reported. Some projects may leave the state entirely, perhaps moving to Louisiana or Georgia—or perhaps going nowhere.
“She would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for data centers,” Johnson’s note said. “The question now is how long the pause lasts.” As PIMCO head of public policy Libby Cantrill similarly warned, “even if statewide moratoria do not result, we expect to see a lot more sand in the gears of the AI buildout regardless—with more time required to secure permits and other approvals, as well as more concessions that data center developers will have to make.”

report.summary: US voters passed 38 of 44 data center restrictions and elected anti-AI candidates like Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, throwing Trump's rapid AI buildout into doubt.
report.background: The Trump administration staked its tech agenda on speed: permitting reform, tax incentives and light regulation to rush gigawatts of data center capacity online, with Texas expected to host over 41 percent of new capacity by 2028. But the physical costs of that boom—strain on household electricity bills, water use, air quality, land and property rights—have landed on local communities faster than any federal benefit arrived. Over the past two years, grassroots opposition has shifted from scattered zoning disputes to organized ballot campaigns and state-level politics. Big Tech's preferred explanation, per reporting on the election fallout, is that this is partisan anti-Trump sentiment rather than anti-tech sentiment—a framing that lets companies avoid conceding that voters object to the industry's own externalities. Either way, the outcome is the same: the binding constraint on AI growth is moving from chips and capital to permits and politics.
key_points: Ballot measures were a rout: of 44 data center initiatives across 10 states, 38 passed, including dozens of moratoriums and outright bans. Even the lone measure that let a project proceed required developer-funded independent reviews and public hearings in a North Dakota city—a signal that 'approval' now comes with concessions.

Texas flipped: Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor's race promising to pause projects until legislation addresses water, electricity, air and property rights. Roughly 13 gigawatts of data center capacity is now exposed, with Bloomberg reporting developers facing a 'worst-case scenario' in the AI boom's epicenter.

Timelines slip, not just plans: analysts expect approved and under-construction sites to keep moving through 2027, so the pain hits 2028 pipelines. Projects with power but no state environmental permits could slip 12-18 months; some may relocate to Louisiana or Georgia, or stall entirely.

'Sand in the gears' regardless: even without statewide moratoriums, PIMCO and other analysts expect longer permitting, more approvals and more concessions from developers. Big Tech's claim that backlash is anti-Trump rather than anti-tech doesn't change the arithmetic on cost and schedule.
report.impact: The AI industry's bottleneck is shifting from GPUs to grid interconnects and county commissions. Hyperscalers and neoclouds should expect higher financing costs, slower revenue recognition on 2028 capacity and a real chance that some announced gigawatt deals never get built—bad news for anyone modeling AI compute supply as elastic. Developers and startups will feel it as scarce, pricier inference capacity, longer queues for colocation and pressure toward efficiency, smaller models and edge deployment rather than brute-force scale. For regular users, the near-term effect is likely subtler: slower price declines, possible rationing or usage caps during peak demand, and rising household utility bills as data center load gets socialized. Politically, AI is now a local-election issue, so expect more candidates campaigning against data centers—and more companies learning to negotiate with communities instead of lobbying past them.
report.tools: For readers tracking this shift, watch GridStatus.io (open-source grid and interconnection data), EIA's electricity demand and capacity reports, and Data Center Map for facility siting. Climate TRACE and WattTime track emissions and marginal grid intensity; the DOE's transmission interconnection queues and state PUC dockets show real permitting timelines. Locally, municipal planning-commission agendas and ballotpedia's data center measure trackers are the earliest warning system—often ahead of national press coverage.
